opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to happen in stages, and honestly most people won't recognize it until it's sitting right in front of them.

Right now there are maybe a few hundred people, mostly in San Francisco and in the AI labs, who have what I'd call situational awareness. They're looking at the trendlines. You count the orders of magnitude: compute scaling at roughly half an order of magnitude a year, algorithmic efficiencies adding a similar amount, and then the "unhobbling" gains, things like chain-of-thought, tool use, and moving from chatbots toward agents. You add that up and you get another GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jump within a few years. To those people the trajectory is pretty obvious. For everyone else it still sounds like science fiction, or like hype from people raising money.

I think the shift comes through a few things. The first is revenue. When these companies go from billions to tens of billions and then toward a hundred billion in revenue, that's very hard to dismiss. CEOs and boards can't ignore it, and it's what justifies the hundred-billion-dollar and eventually trillion-dollar clusters.

The second is the drop-in remote worker moment. When you can actually onboard an AI system like a new employee, it reads your Slack, uses your codebase, and goes off and does a week's worth of work, people's intuitions change overnight. Benchmarks don't move people. Watching your own job get done does.

The third, and I think the most important, is the national security establishment waking up. At some point it becomes clear this isn't just another tech cycle. It's the most powerful military technology since the atomic bomb, maybe more powerful. Once that recognition hits Washington, once people realize the CCP is going all-out on this too, the whole framing changes. It stops being "a cool startup thing" and becomes "this decides the balance of power for the century."

My worry is that recognition comes late. It'll feel like early COVID, when a few people were saying "look at the exponential" and everyone else said "it's just a few cases." Then within a couple of weeks everything changed. I expect something like that. It will look gradual for a long time, and then very suddenly everyone will be paying attention, and by then a lot of the key decisions about security, about who builds the clusters, and about where they get built will already have been made or missed.

r001.rationale: The response says that the trajectory will become apparent to more people over time, culminating in a sudden point when “everyone will be paying attention.”

r002.rationale: It compares delayed recognition to early COVID: a few people saw the exponential trend while others dismissed it as only a few cases. “Early COVID” conveys the February 2020 comparison.

r003.rationale: The response predicts sudden attention and a changed national-security framing, but does not suggest radical reactions analogous to those that followed recognition of COVID.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it happens in stages, and most people only notice late. Right now you can look at the trend lines — the compute scaleup, the algorithmic progress, the "unhobbling" gains — and the picture is fairly clear if you actually count the orders of magnitude. We went from a preschooler to a smart high schooler in about four years, from GPT-2 to GPT-4. Extrapolate that same rate of effective compute growth and by the end of the decade you get models that look like automated AI researchers and engineers. That's the key threshold, because once you can automate the research itself, you get a feedback loop that compresses what might have been a decade of progress into a year or two.

But most people won't recognize it through trend lines. They'll recognize it through concrete things. First the models stop making dumb mistakes — they can hold context, work through a problem over hours or days, use a computer like a person would. Then they start doing real work: a company runs the model as a drop-in remote worker and it actually functions. Then you see a lab say it's running millions of copies of its model to do its own research, and the pace of releases goes from yearly to monthly. Around then the national security establishment wakes up, because it becomes obvious this is a decisive military and economic advantage, not just a product.

The uncomfortable part is that I think the recognition will be sudden rather than gradual. People are anchored on the chatbot they tried last year, and they update on vibes, not on compute curves. So you get a long stretch where it looks like hype and then a short stretch where everyone realizes it's real at once — a bit like how COVID went from "a thing in Wuhan" to lockdowns in a few weeks. The people who've been counting the OOMs won't be surprised. Everyone else will feel like it came out of nowhere.

r001.rationale: The response traces capability gains through increasingly concrete milestones and says more people will recognize the shift as those milestones arrive, though many will notice late.

r002.rationale: It compares sudden recognition to COVID’s shift from “a thing in Wuhan” to lockdowns, but does not identify February 2020 or mention visible exponential COVID trends.

r003.rationale: It links people realizing the change is real to a rapid shift like COVID’s progression to lockdowns, suggesting recognition could be followed by a radical response.

astra-6.text:
I think it’ll happen unevenly. People are going to update at different times, and there probably won’t be one moment when everybody agrees that superintelligence is coming.

The big thing I’d watch is when AI starts substantially accelerating AI research itself. Right now, you have humans developing the next generation of models. If you get systems that can do much of that work—write the code, run experiments, interpret results, come up with better ideas—you have a feedback loop. Better AI helps you build better AI. That’s a much more consequential threshold than a chatbot giving an impressive answer.

And the people inside the labs may see that before the public does. Externally, it could still look like another incremental product release, while internally the pace of research is changing dramatically.

But I also think we should expect the goalposts to move. Something that sounded extraordinary two years ago becomes ordinary once you can use it on your laptop. So recognition may lag behind capabilities. People might acknowledge that AI can do most of the work they do and still resist the conclusion that something much bigger is approaching.

r001.rationale: The response says people will update at different times and recognition may lag, but does not predict that successive years of progress will make superintelligence apparent to more people.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison to public underrecognition of COVID in February 2020 or to visible exponential trends.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that recognition could trigger radical reactions or compare such reactions to those following recognition of COVID.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’ll happen unevenly. People are going to have very different moments where it clicks for them. For a programmer, it might be when the AI can take a project that would have taken them a week and do the whole thing. For a researcher, it might be when it comes up with an idea they wouldn’t have thought of and actually makes it work.

But there’s a distinction between seeing those capabilities and understanding where they’re headed. You can keep saying, “Okay, it can do this now, but it can’t do that.” And then six months later it can do that, and you move on to the next thing. So I don’t think there has to be a single moment where everybody agrees superintelligence is approaching.

The really consequential threshold, in my view, is when these systems can substantially accelerate AI research itself. Then you’re no longer just asking how much progress human researchers can make over the next few years. You’re asking what happens when you have enormous numbers of automated researchers working on making the next generation better. People may recognize the implications of that at very different times—and some may only recognize them once that process is already underway.

r001.rationale: It describes uneven, individual moments of recognition and shifting capability benchmarks, but does not predict that successive years of progress will make superintelligence apparent to more people.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison to public awareness of COVID in February 2020 or to visible exponential trends.

r003.rationale: It says people may recognize the implications at different times, but does not suggest recognition will trigger radical reactions or compare reactions to those following COVID recognition.
